name: AI News
blurb: Daily AI news from the publishers who broke it, split into headline coverage of the field and vendor announcements from the companies building it. Every story links to the original source, and any claim quoted in our coverage is cross-referenced against the laws, lawsuits, companies, tools, papers, and people already tracked in this atlas.

domains.name: AI Headline News
domains.blurb: The day's most consequential AI stories across law, policy, research, safety, and society, curated from 34 vetted feeds. Each item carries the original publisher link and a note on how it connects to the bills, cases, and frameworks tracked elsewhere on this site.

domains.name: AI Vendor News
domains.blurb: Product launches, model releases, pricing changes, and company announcements from the AI vendors themselves. Each item links to the vendor's original announcement and cross-references the company's profile in our AI Companies directory where one exists.

domains.name: This Week in AI
domains.blurb: A weekly record of what moved in AI policy and litigation, permalinked by ISO week.

domains.name: AI Historical Timeline
domains.blurb: From the 1940s to the present: Turing, the perceptron, expert systems, backpropagation, deep learning, AlexNet, transformers, and what followed.

reading.body:
Daily AI news aggregated from 34 vetted feeds covers law, policy, research, safety, and society, with every claim cross-referenced to tracked laws, lawsuits, companies, tools, papers, and people.

The structure separates headline coverage from vendor announcements because the two serve different purposes. Headline news tracks what is happening to the field from outside it: regulatory action, academic breakthroughs, incidents, and policy shifts. Vendor news tracks what companies are doing to the field: product launches, model releases, pricing moves. Both link to original sources. Both cross-reference to other parts of this atlas so a reader can follow a claim backward to its foundation.

This separation matters because the incentives differ. A vendor announces what it believes will drive adoption or reassure regulators. Publishers report what they believe readers need to know. Neither is dishonest, but neither is complete. A reader following both sees the gap between what the field says about itself and what external observers say about the field. That gap is often where the real story lives.

The data does not yet include the historical timeline or indicate what the timeline will contain. It covers the present forward and the week in systematic form. It does not measure which stories move regulation, which move compute decisions, or which are most read. It does not show whether the 510 pages of headline news represent growing or shrinking coverage of AI, or whether that coverage concentrates on certain domains over others.
